entries.title: Nathan Fielder’s Surprise Call From Elizabeth Holmes: ‘I Trust You’
entries.summary: The codirector of “You Can See Everything” talks exclusively to WIRED about truth, lies, and Theranos.
entries.content:
A few months ago, Nathan Fielder’s publicist sent me an unexpected email: Would WIRED be interested in Fielder for a fall cover of our magazine?

The answer, before we even got a reason, was yes. The reason, it turned out, was that Fielder would soon release a project that was so top-secret, I’d need to sign an NDA to even hear about what it was—let alone watch it. I signed, I heard, and then I saw, counting myself among the few dozen people who’d screened You Can See Everything before the film debuted in the first days of September as a secret addition to the Telluride Film Festival.

If you’re a human being with internet access, you know that the buzz following Telluride was nothing short of an online thermonuclear event: Reddit forums exploded; best-in-class memes were born overnight; every journalist on planet Earth, including the staff at WIRED (who had no idea their boss was NDA’d to hell, and seemed confused when I ordered them repeatedly not to contact Nathan Fielder’s publicist), pined, pleaded, and jockeyed for access to the film. Or, even better, for access to Fielder himself. The notoriously inscrutable performer, after all, has become a cult hero for his ability to turn human discomfort into high art. He built a coffee shop called Dumb Starbucks, creating an international news event in the process. He built an entire fake bar so that one man could practice having a difficult conversation with a friend. He trained to be a commercial airline pilot—lunacy!—and flew a 737 filled with passengers (the Miracle over the Mojave), in what can only be described as the most transcendent moment of television I’ve ever seen. For a certain genre of viewer, Nathan Fielder is a comedic god among us mere mortals.

He’s also, not surprisingly, rather particular. Fielder was going to do the cover of WIRED; then maybe he wasn’t. A week went by. Our features director and I didn’t sleep. Then we were a “go.” Great! For a few days, at least, until things got dicey again. This kind of back-and-forth is a normal part of booking celebrities. But given the secrecy, the buzz, the Nathan of it all—the stakes for WIRED were high. I told several people in my life that I hated Nathan Fielder. Then we were on again. I told several people in my life that I loved Nathan Fielder.

You might be wondering: If I found Fielder’s pre-interview agita so stressful, why didn’t we just scrap the cover entirely? Maybe see if Aaron Sorkin was still available, or some other guy involved in some other tech-adjacent fall movie. There are plenty.

The thing is, You Can See Everything is a singularly astonishing film. I’d go so far as to say that it’s among the best I’ve ever seen. Codirected by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it begins as a strange, captivating, occasionally hilarious 34-day psychological dance between Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, and her partner Billy Evans before Holmes’ incarceration, and subsequently morphs into something so beguiling and brilliant that it’s futile to try to describe. After screening You Can See Everything in early September, I thought about the movie every single day until I saw it again a few weeks later. I’m still rolling it around in my brain. When a small handful of WIRED staffers screened the film before Fielder’s cover shoot, we spent hours afterward debating facial expressions, relationships, and even the meaning of single sentences. We agreed on very little, other than that Fielder—notorious for his meticulous building of worlds—seemed to have finally stumbled into one much stranger than anything he could have conjured.

When I ultimately sat down with Fielder for a conversation in late September, any lingering irritation at his pre-interview jitters instantly fell away: For all of his overthinking, lines in the sand, and apparent ambivalence to press, Fielder presented as considerate and genuine. Over nearly an hour and a half, Fielder—in trademark New Balance sneakers and nondescript men’s apparel, a Summit Ice windbreaker in tow—slumped casually on a sofa, seemed to mull my questions earnestly and in good faith, and did the best he possibly could to answer them. Verbal communication, Fielder repeated several times in our conversation, isn’t always easy for him. It’s a quality that’s often put to good use in his work, and his blunt demeanor makes Fielder particularly effective in the role of truth-seeker vis-à-vis Holmes and Evans. The same can’t be said for a sit-down interview, which made my conversation with Fielder all the more endearing in the moment; at least, I told myself, the man was really trying.

Our time together concluded at 2:17 pm; I’d been warned beforehand that Fielder had a Zoom meeting at 2:15 pm sharp. “I’m trusting you,” his publicist told me before leaving us alone to talk. I took the entreaty seriously, practically shoving Fielder out of the room as soon as I realized he was running late. This lovely, thoughtful man has a meeting! Days later, a thought gnawed at me: 2:15 pm is an odd time to start a meeting. On a Sunday, no less.

I couldn’t shake it. Had the publicist looked me in the eyes and lied? Had Nathan? I considered asking them outright. I’ve never been one for ambiguity, and a journalist craves nothing more than to know what’s real. Then again, people make things up all the time. They present different versions of themselves to different people, obfuscate and perform, and they do it in little ways and sometimes bigger ones. Did it really matter if he’d left for a real meeting or the excuse of one? And hadn’t I spent enough time letting Nathan Fielder make me feel crazy?

In the end, I decided that this time it was better not to know. It was better just to trust. And after a second talk with Fielder a few weeks after our first conversation, I learned that Elizabeth Holmes might feel the same way.

The interview has been edited for clarity.

KATIE DRUMMOND: I have a lot of anxiety about recording interviews.

NATHAN FIELDER: Why? About losing the recording?

Yeah.

OK. You have a backup too.

I have two.

I would do the same thing.

Do you?

What?

Double-record things?

No, but if I had your job, I would.

OK. Before we get into it, I just want you to know that I know how important it is for you to preserve the experience of the film.

Yes. But you know, some people enjoy knowing what happens. I read this thing where they told people the end of a story, and then they had another group that didn’t know, and then the group that knew the ending said they enjoyed it more.

So it could just be a me thing. Maybe it is. But I love being surprised. I love the experience of just sort of not knowing.

When this interview comes out, the film will be just out in theaters. But it was a secret for three years, right?

Yeah.

My understanding is that only a few dozen people knew it was happening.

We kept it really small.

Secrecy has been a feature of your work before. What made you decide to keep it so under wraps? Why was that important to you?

I think, firstly, it was a concern on the subjects’ part. No one knew where they were at first. But while we were shooting there, paparazzi started surrounding the location and all that. So one of the understandings was, we needed to keep it secret because it could affect things with them, and we didn’t want to do anything where our involvement would be a news story or change things with them.

In addition to that, I think when stuff comes out about a thing, then the narrative is out there, and it may affect our ability to make the project. We didn’t know who we wanted to talk to or get on camera. We didn’t have a plan when we went in, so we were just like, “It’s best to operate in a place where no one knows it exists.” We thought it would be a net benefit.

How many people did you have to lie to about this?

I didn’t lie as much as say, “Oh, I can’t talk about this thing I’m working on, but I really want you to see it when it’s out.” People knew I was working on something. My family knew, people I’m close with that are trusted friends and collaborators.

And now there’s a teaser out. There’s a trailer. That’s about it. How did you think about the lead-up to the film? Was that strategic in terms of deciding what to put out there and what not to?

Is this strategic? I don’t know. I think everyone didn’t really know how to handle this.

Even people at A24 didn’t know we were making this for a bit, because we just went and started doing it, and so it wasn’t really on their radar in terms of what it’s gonna look like. Then, they’re the pros on how to release a movie. I think they saw an opportunity in doing it all at once at Telluride. I was like, "Will that be enough time?" Because they normally have a long lead time when they first do these movie things. It was gonna give us five weeks until it was released.

Oh, wow.

They felt confident in their plan. And then it was a question of what we put out there. We got the sense pretty early on that she’s a very toxic figure to people everywhere, so I understood that we were dealing with material that people were gonna project a lot onto. I think everyone thought that maybe the audience will meet us halfway with some of the stuff we put out.

Have you been reading the speculation? Are you reading—

Speculation about what?

About the film, from everyone who hasn’t seen it.

What are people speculating? I haven’t seen.

Theories that she’s naked, that you’re naked, that—

Oh that.

—that you dress up as Elizabeth Holmes, that you become her. I saw an image someone made of you with a blonde wig on.

I haven’t seen a lot of that stuff. When this all came out and we did the Telluride Film Festival, my phone was off for that whole night, and then I started looking at some stuff the next day, but there was a lot, and it was a little overwhelming. I couldn’t really engage with everything. I definitely understand that people would project stuff onto a new project that feels like stuff I’ve done in the past. But this is a totally unique thing. It feels, to me, so different than what I’ve done before in the way it came together, in the way it functions, and what we’re able to explore in it.

I’ve never done something like this before, but the process was fascinating, and I really enjoyed shooting this way. It was a real freeing and fascinating experience.

What was freeing about it?

Well, for example, I think a lot of projects usually have to be generated by you. You have a concept, and you go and pitch that concept, and then you have to present a plan to get the money to make it, and then you go and execute it. Things can change while you’re doing it, but usually if they green-light a project, you have to deliver something.

Ideally.

Yes. You can’t—

You seem like someone who plans quite a bit.

I mean, I try to. I try to plan, and then I’m always met with the absurdity of me trying to plan too much. I experienced that when I did Nathan for You. I was trying to be like, “OK, we can know where things would go.” But then the best moments were when we’re just totally surprised by something we didn’t expect, and then we end up going in that direction. And the aftermath of that was like, “Why did I think I could predict or control that?”

That was part of the inspiration for The Rehearsal—that tendency that I have to want to, like, plan. There is a pressure sometimes of, “you have to deliver something,” so you want to think things through. You can’t just go into something.

But with this, because I came into this feeling like the story’s been told about her, I was very interested in meeting her, but I did not see what a film about her or a project about her could be.

You and Lance reached out to her initially, right?

It was a bit of a both thing, because she and Billy [Evans] had approached A24 with the desire to have their life documented in some way. But no one was attached. It’s just them approaching A24. And I guess the negotiations fell apart because there was nothing to it, really.

Months later, I heard that that had happened. So I called A24 and said, “Well, could I meet her?” That was the start of it all.

Why her for you? Why did she seem interesting?

It’s a good question. Sometimes I don’t know why I’m drawn to something. But I had read Bad Blood.

Yeah.

I was really interested in that book when it came out, and I thought her relationship to the media was interesting too, because she sort of went silent and didn’t talk to anyone about anything in the aftermath. I was just personally curious. Like, “I wonder what this person’s like.”

And also, why now? Why is she wanting to speak and have her life documented and do it in this way? And even after I met her, if I didn’t know what I knew, I would just think I was talking with a very affable, soft-spoken, kind person. But then I kept having this thing where I was tracking my thoughts about how honest she was being, or if I was being manipulated in some way.

The feeling is so odd. It felt like watching a magician. I talk about it a little in the film, but when me and Lance were first talking about her, we happened to be at the Magic Castle. I’m a member, and it just came up that way. It was sort of poetic. I told A24, “I don’t really know what the angle is, but there is something tickling in my brain.”

She was about to go to prison, so we didn’t know what was gonna happen. I was like, “If you guys want, I’m down to go down and start filming and see what emerges. But we need the ability to deliver nothing to you guys if it doesn’t work out.” And they said sure.

So was that freeing?

Yes. It really meant I didn’t have to hold back with her or with them. Making a film or making any project is very stressful. So if we had to pull the plug because it didn’t work out, it would sort of be a relief to me. It’s a very nice zone to operate in. Lance and I both thought, “Well, at the very least, this will be an interesting week or two that we’ll have as a story.”

I’ve seen it a few times. As I was watching it recently, I found myself trying to figure out: What did Elizabeth and Billy think they were bringing you in to tell? What was the story that they thought had not been told?

Yeah. Right?

Do you know? Do you feel like you know why they wanted you in their home, in their life?

This is a question that we are still debating to this day. Me and my editor, Adam Locke-Norton, who has worked with me on The Rehearsal and for years—we were debating exactly this.

Because it keeps changing. The difficult thing about this whole thing is there are so many pieces, and some of them are contradictory. You have to have a mindset of someone playing 7D chess with you, and they are so far ahead to make sense of all this stuff that it almost seems implausible sometimes.

Did you worry that they were ahead of you?

I didn’t worry, because I’m there, and I’m just trying to experience it and let my curiosity drive me. The first couple days, we were trying to figure out how to capture this and what they were gonna give us and what they were trying to do. We didn’t really know. We didn’t know if we would sit in there and they’d bring out papers and lay out a whole thing or they’d just be like, “We’re just gonna live our life.” They weren’t immediately coming to us with some sort of narrative they were trying to push. So we realized it was this game of figuring this out in a way.

We ended up having this plan where we would come in every morning. We started with two cameras, and we eventually got to three cameras, and we had one that was on a 12-millimeter-wide lens that could get the whole main area of the house. And then we had two other cameras that were on 25- to 250 [millimeter] zoom lenses, so they could go wide, but they could also go really tight. And we’d place them in the far ends of the house. We found these angles where if anything happened at any point in the house, we could not only have it in our wide shot, but then we could get it in close-ups eventually.

We only had two camera operators. Lance wouldn’t always be in there. He would sometimes be outside with the monitor. So sometimes there were only three people, and our sound guy who’d sometimes be outside. I could definitely sense that she felt the stakes were high for her, and that can cause people to be unnatural in ways that they may not be in real life.

That’s a part of the work I make. I like to show how the cameras can affect how people are, a little bit. That feels the most honest way to do things. With this project as well, we were really trying to show how she is, even when the cameras aren’t there.

When did you realize that you needed to be in it?

That’s another thing. I started this thing being like, “I’m definitely not gonna be on camera in this.” The situation was very intense. She was going to prison. And that’s another thing about having the ability to pull the plug on the project with no consequences, why it was really nice for me, because I could also say to both of them—if I did sense there was tension or stress about this whole thing—I was very aware this is the final month that she’s gonna have for a decade with her kids and her family.

I said almost every day, "If ever you’re regretting this decision, just tell me and we’ll go. Like, no problem." I’d usually bring it up if there was tension, because sometimes we’d be trying to do shoots, and Billy would be trying to stop it or just be like, “That’s enough time.”

So I was like, “We don’t have to be here at all, but if we’re gonna be here, we just wanna be able to do this.” They never once said, “OK, we don’t want you here anymore” or seemed to be like, “OK, let me think about if we wanna change our minds.” That was confusing for me too. Because it didn’t make sense to me. I definitely would not want a camera crew following me for the last month of freedom that I would have.

Not only would I not want a camera crew, I don’t know that I would want you there.

Are you feeling that because of the conversation we’ve had so far?

No, but I would—

You’re saying I’m worse than the average person.

No, I would’ve seen your earlier work and the way you observe people and behavior, and I’d be very stressed out at the prospect of Nathan Fielder being in my house.

Yeah. This is part of the mystery that, like, doesn’t make sense to me.

No offense, but why you? You know what I mean?

Yeah. I asked her that on, I think, one of the first days we shot. I still don’t fully understand it. That really messed with my head. Also, I got the sense very early that she hadn’t seen a lot, but she had seen some of what I did, and she had talked to people who had seen what I did. Billy had seen more. I think she found the clip that she said she saw funny.

But you know, her relationship to that … to what’s funny? I don’t even know. She said her favorite movie is Elf, the Will Ferrell movie. You have the tattoo—

It’s actually my daughter’s initials, but I get that a lot.

Do you love that movie?

I like that movie well enough.

OK. So you and her there.

I like it well enough.

What areas do you feel like you’re similar to her, besides liking Elf? Or in what ways?

To Elizabeth Holmes?

Yeah.

I don’t like where this interview is going. But we’re both convicted felons, with a long track record of fraudulent behavior. We both had children to avoid prison time. We have that in common.

Do you feel those things about her?

Everything I just said?

Well, I guess you said various things. Some things are obviously true.

We both have blue eyes. I believe that her eye color is real.

Here’s a question. How do people view her? I’m assuming WIRED is very in with the tech world—

Yeah.

How did people view that, at the time, in that world? And how do people view it now, and is it the same, or has that changed?

There’s this broader culture of Silicon Valley that she operated within, where everyone’s a liar. You start a company, you lie, you fake it till you make it, and VCs expect it, and it is part and parcel of launching a business. Elon Musk is an incredible liar—lies to the public, lies to regulators, lies to lawmakers, investors, shareholders. That’s part of the game. And she, to me, in many ways, played that same game.

She did it to the nth degree; she took it very far. But what she was doing at the time was very much in keeping with what startup founders do. They go out, they raise money, they talk a big game, they get magazine covers. I think today, if you ask any journalist, whether they’re a tech journalist or not, they’d say she’s a convicted felon. She’s a fraud. And I think the first time I saw the film—now I’m going on a bit of a tangent, and I’m going to have to start asking you questions again soon, but—

No, I’m really curious, though. I hadn’t thought about Theranos in a long time, right?

Yeah, I think a lot of people coming into this haven’t thought about Elizabeth Holmes in five, six, seven years.

Yeah.

I have a 9-year-old daughter, and watching Holmes with her kids in the first half of the film, I felt tremendous empathy for this woman. I was asking myself a lot of questions about her romantic relationships and wondering whether that was at the root of it all along. I wondered if there was something wrong with her. Cognitively wrong with her.

And then I was getting ready to do this interview, and so I read back about everything she had done, about the timing of when she had kids. I went to screen the movie a second time and felt like such a fucking dupe for being close to tears watching her with her little kids. I still feel sad for the kids, but I felt much less empathy for her. I would say, broadly within the journalism community, Bad Blood was the definitive reported account of what she did.

Mm.

But I think watching the movie brings a lot to the surface for the viewer and raises a lot of questions about her and her character and what’s influencing her and what motivates her. What was I asking you? How rude of you to distract me.

It’s interesting for me, I think, because I couldn’t really talk to people about this fully while I was making it, besides the people that we were there with.

How did you process on a daily basis what you were experiencing?

In a way, we processed it with each other. One of the reasons early on that we felt this could actually be a project was because of what came out of those processing sessions. At the end of the day, I would have in my head what I thought was a very clear idea of what was happening, and Lance or our camera guy, Jonathan Mitchell, or our DP, David Bolen, or our sound guy, Richard Carlos, they would all have a different take on what actually happened.

I was like, how is this possible? We’re all in this room experiencing this thing. We’re all witnessing something and having a different idea of what’s going on. And I thought that was a basic premise to explore and chase.

At Telluride, you said that you still don’t know what you experienced. You want audiences to help you understand. What specifically do you want to hear from people after this comes out?

I generally don’t see myself as having a great framework for understanding all the variables of things and people. In a lot of the work I do, because it’s shorter or television sometimes, you have to take a human that’s very complex, obviously, with a lot of nuance in a lot of different areas, and you’re generally trying to simplify. You have to be like, “OK, well, this is the essence of the situation or the person, or this is an interesting flavor of them, and that’s what we’re gonna show.”

But with this, we’re really trying to give the viewer everything. We’re trying to focus on these moments that we couldn’t really make sense of fully. Like I was saying, still to this day, I’m debating. Why are me and my editor talking, two days ago, about trying to understand certain things? I’ve talked to people who have seen it, and they’re all bringing out new ideas that I would never even consider.

So you trust the audience.

I just think people are smart. I don’t see myself as the most knowledgeable at everything, and I love learning from the world and from people. I definitely don’t come to anything being like, “I know what the answers are” or “I know what things are.” Just in general, not with this project. When I was in grade six maybe, or grade seven, I was with a tutor, and they were like, “I think you know probably less than 200 words.” And I was like, “No, I know more than that.” I started naming them. I started trying to count, because I was insecure that I didn’t know as much as others or something. But now I think I’ve grown into being comfortable with anything I don’t know. I think it drives a lot of my curiosity, and probably why I hate you asking me questions.

You hate this right now?

I want to set this thing up so people can watch this in the right way. I want people to go and see the film, because that’s what I want to express. You know? It’s the film. So that’s why I’m more curious about your experiences—because you can think you know something, and then you start talking to a lot of people, and then you’re like, “Oh, I actually know nothing.” Anyways.

No, it’s funny. It’s—

I’m not even sure if what I just said made any sense at all.

I get what you’re saying.

This is not my skill set, like articulating with words, as a verbal storyteller.

Sure.

I can do things with how I’ve learned to do them visually.

Yeah.

OK.

That’s fine.

But this is your medium. You’re good at doing this. You do the storytelling like this.

I do my best.

Yes.

That’s what I do. How do you feel like you know Elizabeth Holmes? You spent a lot of time with her …

I didn’t answer your question. What was it? I remember what you asked me, about being on camera.

That was 20 minutes ago.

But I went on a tangent about how we filmed it.

I do want to know, when did you decide you had to be in the film?

I was talking about that process of where we put the cameras, and how we did it to get to this. Because what would happen is they would be living their life and doing things, and we would try to capture these things.

But then a couple things started happening. Firstly, because I was there, they would keep engaging with me. So they would be talking to each other, but then they would be like, "Nathan, what do you think?" And I would chime in from off camera. Or if nothing was really happening, I would ask a question to see what they would say about something. But I was off camera, and it was more to prompt a discussion or something like that. Or they would start talking to me, and conversations would go on for long enough that the operators started panning over to me.

But also, they would say stuff that tickled a part of my brain that was like, “Something’s off about this.” Or I feel like this is them trying to do some sort of propaganda. So I would wanna interject to be like, “Well, actually, I read this,” or “I thought this was the case.” We realized, “Oh, someone has to push back, and we can’t just let them run whatever show they kinda wanna do.”

Now back to my most recent question.

OK.

Do you feel like you know Elizabeth? You spent so much time with this woman. You lived in their home.

Well, I know her better than I did going in. Sure. I knew nothing about her.

How much about her had you read and watched before you showed up? Did you go in with this canon of Elizabeth Holmes reporting and filmmaking?

I’d read the book. Which I thought was the main document. And then when we started doing it, I listened to the ABC podcast they did on the trial, but I was sort of cramming it. I would go home, I would listen to more.

As we were there, I would just be like, “OK, I’m trying to digest everything I can.” But at the same time, I’m not a science journalist. This isn’t my specialty, so I was also aware that I may not be able to go into certain areas with her, but I could approach her through other means.

I felt like I knew enough to know when something didn’t feel right. I definitely had engaged enough with that, but I was digesting more and more as time went on. I don’t know. That’s such a crazy concept—knowing enough, I’m realizing. It’s like, what does that even mean?

Well, yeah. How do you know that you ever really know someone is kind of a big—

Oh, well, that … Yeah. I mean, in terms of knowing her, I’m like—

Do you feel like you know her as a real person? Like a person person, not the character of Elizabeth Holmes, the fraud that everybody has read about. Is there a different version there?

I think because she’s someone that has limited her presence—she hasn’t done a lot of interviews, and she has really limited her engagement with the media in general—I think the version that is out there of her is largely a version that people are putting together from the pieces they have. The first time I met her, I was like, “This is not how I thought she would be.”

How did you think she would be?

I guess I expected a little more outward anxiety and a desire to control.

She wasn’t controlling?

That was very jarring for me, because she did not come across as controlling. I thought the situation that she was in, there would be a lot about it. We’re in this tiny beach house. That’s a tense environment. The weird thing is that she let us come there without trying to be like, “OK, well, what’s your angle? What are you gonna do here? What is this interview gonna be about?” You know, there wasn’t that stuff, and I totally expected we would get all that.

And that, I think, messed with my head as well. Is that intentional? Or is there some design to this whole thing that I’m not aware of, and I’m in some hall of mirrors that I am not even conscious of?

It was a wild experience, but one thing I feel like I really know is her tendencies. We’re talking about spending 12 hours, 18 hours a day, with this person in all these different environments. I feel like I know how she would handle any situation or what she would act like or say in response to something. Can I say something off the record?

[Goes off the record.]

You were saying you felt like you knew her so well in a certain way. But what is it like to feel that way but also grapple with the fact that she may have been lying to you the entire time?

We’re back on.

Yeah.

It almost feels, at times, that it’s not so black-and-white what’s going on in her head. A lie, a classic lie, is someone who’s like, “OK, I am saying something that I’m consciously knowing is not true in this moment.” But it’s not just the words, it’s the design of every aspect of her life that feels like a part of what is going on. What’s interesting about her to me, I think, just goes beyond that in any given moment … I can’t piece it together. She makes these claims that are like—how could anyone believe this or say they’ve never done this? Is it a lie in that moment? Is it a lie if she believes it to be true?

One thing that’s interesting about this situation with her is that I don’t think she believed she was going to prison until very close to her going.

How is that possible?

They were working on an appeal. There was a sense that something maybe was gonna happen that would cause her not to go.

I don’t know if I find that endearing or just so—what’s the word? Just the arrogance of it, the delusional arrogance of it.

I guess it’s a question of, what is the level you’re supposed to operate at in terms of how positively or negatively you’re supposed to think about anything in your life? When you think about future events, is it healthier to be like, “I see my future as this happy place that’s going to be great and great things are gonna happen,” or is it better to be like, “There are all these things that might be bad, and I need to be ready and I need to understand that that is a possible reality”? What is the balance?

I’m going into zones that are not my expertise. You should talk to a psychologist about this stuff.

I think if I was going to prison in two weeks, I would understand and accept that I was going to prison in two weeks.

Her prison date shifted at one point, so I don’t know if it puts these things in your head where it’s a possibility. But with everyone, there’s a gap between what they think the future will be and what it really is, the actual odds. How often is anyone aligned with the actual odds of, like, a future thing happening? But people who are positive, people who are optimistic generally, don’t stew in the negatives, right?

She can come across as a very positive person. She focuses on those positive things. The idea of, “Maybe I’m not going to prison.”

You mentioned a few minutes ago that you did not find her to be controlling.

Just to correct, she didn’t appear to be controlling.

She didn’t appear to be.

That was my sense. But then—yeah, go ahead.

I want to ask you about Billy. That’s why I bring it up, because he was a controlling presence in the film, and their relationship is a really important part of it. What was interesting to me is that our creative director, when she saw the film, said, “I just thought it was so interesting how she used her husband in that way.” And I was like, “What are you talking about? He was using her.” We still do not agree about that relationship and what was going on in that marriage.

Oh, I don’t know about [marriage]. They even muddy the waters with that. Like, he’ll call her his wife.

How did you come to understand that relationship?

That came to be a big part of trying to understand her. But I could say certain things right now that would definitely affect how people enter the movie. I would have to talk about some stuff we explore later. I want people to have the experience you had and your colleagues had. Sometimes people are like, “Oh, the filmmaker thought this, so this is the truth.”

One of the great things about the film is that we don’t know what you think. I didn’t feel like I left the movie being like, “Nathan thinks this, this, and this about these people.”

That’s interesting. It’s fascinating to watch it back and watch these moments where I am not even thinking about the production or what’s happening. I see myself fully just being in it with them. A lot of it was like, how is this possible that I’m meeting humans that are talking like this?

Have you heard from either of them, Elizabeth or Billy? I mean, they had certain expectations going into this. They had a story they ostensibly wanted to tell.

Well, I don’t know what their expectations were.

I don’t either, but I have to imagine that they were different than the end result.

Here’s what they said, or what Billy said at times: “I just want people to see the real Elizabeth.” And I felt like we could align on that idea. We were like, “Yes, we are desiring to show as close as we can get.” He might have had a different idea in his head of who the real Elizabeth is, but we could align on the idea of that’s what we’re trying to do.

He may not have realized that they would also see the real Billy.

Yeah. Although I guess you can see pretty early in the film how comfortable he is being a part of this.

Extremely comfortable.

It’s hard to tell. I can’t really project their motives for—

But have you heard from them?

Well, basically near the end of when we were trying to finish it, there was this increased effort, we felt, to control the process and the project from Billy’s perspective. We had to cut off communication. So we haven’t actually spoken with him in a little bit or in the last—what’s the date today?

The 27th.

In the last, like, three weeks.

Has he seen the film?

No. Not to my knowledge. We haven’t shown it to him. I was trying to think if there was a screening that had happened. By the time this comes out, maybe? Or probably? I have no idea.

He’ll probably go on opening weekend.

I don’t know.

There’s a body of work about Elizabeth Holmes that’s already been made. You’re adding to that body of work with this, and I’m curious what you hope to add to the cultural understanding of this person and her story and what she did?

I guess I don’t really think about it on those terms. I think what the movie ended up being to me feels like it goes beyond that in a way. I don’t know what it will do to people’s understanding of her. But people are really complex. I think that’s more a question for you.

Well, I can end the interview for us. I think what you were saying about human behavior, and people being complicated, that’s ultimately what it’s about, right? I think in the context of her, she is seen as a supervillain. She’s almost like a cartoon character in how she’s perceived. The movie reminds us that she’s a person, and people are complicated, and that many things can be true about someone at the same time. Which is hard for me, because I really don’t like ambiguity. But different things can be true about Elizabeth Holmes at the same time.

One thing that’s emerged that’s interesting is the way you and your coworkers are having different ideas of what’s actually happening in this movie. Each of us has our own life and our own experiences, and maybe it’s partially about what we’re bringing to it too.

That’s how it’s gonna hit differently for different people. That’s why I feel like it’s the healthy thing for me to be like, “I don’t know a lot,” or I feel more comfortable in a place where I’m … Ugh, I don’t have the words to describe what I’m feeling right now.

Close your eyes and try again.

I’m gonna give up halfway through this sentence. I think my tutor was right.

That was the end of my interview with Nathan Fielder. As we reviewed the conversation, though, I kept coming away feeling like we were missing an ending. So I asked Fielder for a few more minutes on the phone, and he graciously agreed. We spoke right before the film was released nationally. As it turns out, there was quite a postscript.

How have you been?

I've been pretty OK. How about you? How have you been?

Great. Since we last talked, reviews have started coming in for the movie, and I wondered how you feel about them. And whether you're paying any attention.

No, I haven't. I saw that a bunch of stuff is coming in all at once, and it's a lot, and I haven't had the time to properly engage with it all. But I'm happy people who have seen it seem to be connecting with it so far. But I guess it hasn't gone out to everyone yet, so we'll see.

It goes out nationwide tomorrow, correct?

Yes. Tomorrow. And some places today.

We have some editors going today after work. Are you nervous about the wider public reception?

I am … I am OK. I'm trying to just take it a day at a time, but it's been a long road to get to this point, so, in a way, I'm looking forward to it just finally being something that everyone can engage with.

The last time we talked, almost three weeks ago, you had not heard from Billy, and you had not heard from Elizabeth. Has that changed?

Well, actually—on Friday last week—I looked at my phone in the morning and saw I had two missed calls, and on the voicemail transcript it said that it was a call from the prison.

What?

Yes. And then I saw on the thing, it says: You're receiving a call from Elizabeth Holmes. And I have not heard from her. She has not called me in over six months. I have not heard from her in any way. But I missed the calls, and then as I was looking at my phone, a third call came in from the same number.

Persistent!

I picked it up. She had mentioned at one point, or someone mentioned, that she has to call multiple times [from prison], and you can't call back. So, she has to sometimes do that if people miss calls.

So I answered the phone, and I said, “Hey, how's it going?” She asked how I was doing. I asked her if she had seen any stuff about the film coming out and how she felt about it all. She told me that she had seen some stuff, but most things she just isn't seeing, so she's heard things, but she hasn't really read anything. And then, at the end, she said to me—“I trust you.”

And what did you say to that?

I said, “OK, thanks.”

And then the call ended?

Well, we talked about some other stuff. She talked about her kids, and then some updates that are not really my place to share. But then after that, she said again, at the end of the call—“I trust you.” And I don't know what she meant by that.

I don't know either. I'm actually trying to think about what she might have … I mean, I guess …

She said it twice.

She said it twice. Well, the most superficial explanation is she’s just saying, “I trust you to tell my story.” Whatever version of that story she thinks exists to tell.

I cannot … It would be, I think, wrong to be … This is, again, me just not having the words to even speculate. I don't know.

And so you're thinking about it, and you just don't know?

Well, it's in the context of a call that was out of the blue, and … I don't know, I didn't even know she had an ability to reach out to me anymore, because I haven’t heard anything.

She's trusting you, Nathan. That's what she says.

I like to think it. I like to think I'm a trustworthy guy.

Now you're going into the film release tomorrow with that additional comment from her rolling around in your brain. Is that messing you up at all?

I think it sort of makes it feel in my mind that, like, it's continuing to this day, everything that, like—

Everything that you experienced, that people will see.

Well, there's a lot. It's just the whole thing is hard to unravel, and every piece I try to interpret. I don't want to create too much meaning to any given moment, but then my mind does try to figure those things out.

Just when you think you’re out, she pulls you back in. You might never escape.

It hasn't ended, I guess.

entries.title: How the Xbox’s Disc-to-Digital Program Works
entries.summary: Microsoft is letting players digitize their game discs for free, but don't sell your physical collection just yet.
entries.content:
After Sony announced plans to abandon physical discs by 2028, all eyes turned to Microsoft to see whether its next-gen console, codenamed Project Helix and described as “an open-platform hybrid PC-console,” will continue to support physical media.

Microsoft has largely stayed silent (though there are plenty of reasons to keep an easily accessible 4K Blu-ray drive for consumers). One big hint that Xbox may be gearing up for a disc-less future, though, is the rollout of a feature called Disc to Digital.

The new tool lets players claim digital copies of their Xbox Series X or Xbox One physical games, making them accessible anywhere they can log into their Xbox account. After a month of beta testing for Xbox Insider users, the feature is now open to everyone, and you don't even need an Xbox Game Pass subscription. In theory, it allows anyone to archive their physical collections—but it’s not without a few complications.

Insert Disc to Continue

So, how does it work? It’s almost as easy as just popping the disc into your console, but not quite. Microsoft says “playing any supported Xbox One or Xbox Series X game disc while signed in will grant you a digital license of that game.” In my experience, this didn’t happen automatically when I launched a game disc.

Instead, pressing the menu button while hovering over the game tile on the Xbox home screen brings up an option to “Claim Digital License.” If it’s supported (more on that in a moment), you’ll get a pop-up showing “Digital license unlocked.” Disc-to-Digital games are tied to your Xbox account rather than your console, and appear in your library with a new icon on the game tile, a disc “disintegrating” into bits of data.

You can then install the game and any updates, then play without the disc in the drive. This will start automatically if you have “Play disc automatically” enabled in your system settings: Go to Profile & system > Settings > Devices & connections > Disc, and turn that option off to keep on top of storage space.

Thankfully, claiming digital licenses isn’t restricted to the current-gen Xbox Series X—it also works on Xbox One consoles with a disc drive. If you upgraded to the disc-less Xbox Series S or the all-digital Series X but still have an Xbox One, this opens a new path for backward compatibility: redeem physical games on the last-gen model, then install them digitally on the newer console. Overall, it's a remarkably simple and welcome process.

Keep in mind you can play digital Xbox One games from an external HDD if you're limited on storage, but Xbox Series games must be installed on either the Series X or Series S internal SSD or an official expansion drive. All storage is pricey right now (thanks, AI), but these proprietary format cards are especially so, ranging from $200 for Seagate’s 1-terabyte model to $550 for 4 TB.

Disc Read Error

The main issue? Disc to Digital is far from universal—not every Xbox Series X and Xbox One game disc is supported, and Microsoft doesn't have an official list of which games are.

First-party titles such as Halo, Gears of War, or Forza Horizon are safe bets, but this doesn’t extend to legacy titles—for instance, Fallout 4, released for Xbox One in 2015, can’t be redeemed as a Disc-to-Digital title yet, despite Microsoft acquiring developer Bethesda in 2021. Third-party games are entirely hit and miss. The Warner Bros. Interactive-published The Lego Ninjago Movie Video Game worked, but Capcom’s Dead Rising 3 didn’t.

The language is also confusing about why you might not be able to redeem a game. One disc gave the error “Digital license unavailable: This game is not participating in digital licensing. You can still play with the disc inserted.” Another showed “This disc doesn’t support a digital license: This disc can’t be used to get access to a digital license. This could be because it is an unsupported disc, or because the disc is damaged. You can still play with the disc inserted.” (And I could, putting the damaged disc theory to rest.)

In many cases, this is likely down to Xbox still negotiating with partners to include their titles. As more publishers come on board, expect more compatible discs. Right now though, the lack of clarity on which games can be redeemed, or what happens when they can’t, makes the whole process a crapshoot.

Sadly, this isn’t a golden ticket for all-encompassing backward compatibility, either. It’s strictly limited to Xbox One and Xbox Series games, likely because those consoles have unique identifiers for those discs. Xbox 360 and original Xbox discs didn’t, which could lead to a literal free-for-all of digital licenses if you could ‘rip’ a game and then pass on or sell the disc for someone to do the same.

This does create another point of confusion, though. When you claim the Disc-to-Digital license for a compatible game, you’re told, “Your digital license is linked to your disc. To ensure your digital license stays in your library, keep possession of your game disc.” That sounds contradictory, given the system also removes the need for a disc to play. After all, after claiming the license for Lego Ninjago on my Series X, I installed and played it on my Xbox One without ever inserting the disc.

Microsoft hasn't clarified whether this means the Disc-to-Digital license will need to be renewed by periodically re-inserting the disc. It’s a big “watch this space” for now, but you probably shouldn’t sell off your disc-drive consoles or physical game collections just yet.

Play Anywhere?

The games you can redeem aren’t necessarily accessible across your devices, either. You still need to keep compatibility in mind—you can play newly digitized Xbox One games on an Xbox Series console, but not the reverse. PC players using the Xbox app can install their Disc-to-Digital games if they’re also included in Microsoft’s Play Anywhere catalog. The same applies to Xbox Cloud Gaming—if it’s not in that catalog, you can't play it, even if it's associated with your Xbox account.

Speaking of which, Microsoft recently capped cloud gaming access, saying that “the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it,” glossing over the cost and impact of AI infrastructure on server-side components and service provision. Game Pass Ultimate subscribers are now limited to 15 "free" hours per month, 10 for Premium users, and a meager five for those on the Essential plan. Beyond that, users must purchase additional streaming time through the Xbox Store. Even if your Disc-to-Digital game is in the cloud library, you may not get much play time if you want to run it through Cloud Gaming.

That’s a few caveats to keep in mind, but most of them should improve with time, as Microsoft refines the service. For the most part, Disc to Digital works "out of the box" and provides a great way for players to streamline their collections. It feels timely, too—as game install sizes have exceeded disc capacities, the discs themselves have become glorified installation packs, so why not make them a passkey to the digital version that gets installed anyway?

Whether Disc-to-Digital's arrival means the next Xbox will be entirely digital remains to be seen. Right now, it’s a great feature for Xbox players—easy to use, convenient, and surprisingly consumer-friendly. If Microsoft can build toward universal support, this could be its killer feature … at least for the rest of this console generation.

entries.title: Maricopa County, Arizona, Is Again Ground Zero of Election Conspiracy Theories
entries.summary: In 2020, Maricopa County became the epicenter for Trump’s claims the election was stolen. Six years, later the president and his allies are dusting off their “rigged” playbook ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
“Maricopa is a very, very dishonest county,” President Donald Trump told reporters last week.

One could be forgiven for thinking that you had time-traveled back to the chaotic weeks and months following the 2020 presidential election, when Arizona's Maricopa County became the focal point for the election denial movement.

But Maricopa, and election deniers, are back. With just over two weeks to go before the midterms, extremist election activists are trying to undermine trust in the voting process and are ramping up their efforts to confuse and scare people. Central to this is to fall back on well-known tropes that have been used in the past, including the idea that Maricopa County is somehow corrupt.

“At this point, people are tuned into Maricopa as a focus of election rumors,” Kate Starbird, cofounder of the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington, tells WIRED. “Sharpie pens bleeding through ballots in 2020. Tabulator machines not reading ballots in 2022. Maricopa has become a familiar setting, a place where election issues arise or are perceived to arise, and where those issues get wrapped into ‘rigged election’ conspiracy theories.”

No evidence of widespread voter fraud in Maricopa County has ever been found, but in March of this year, the administration refocused attention on the county when the FBI seized dozens of hard drives and servers containing data from the Cyber Ninjas audit. The attention was intensified last week, when Trump told reporters that election officials in the county should “be ashamed of themselves” after 3,000 ballots were mailed early in error.

But the rumors went into overdrive last weekend when We the People USA Alliance, an election-denial group central to the baseless claims about voter fraud in Maricopa County in 2020, posted a video on X with the caption “BUSTED.”

The video shows two Maricopa County employees working late at night on October 7 inside the ballot tabulation center. The post insinuated that they were tampering with equipment by “inserting flash drives into computers … during an active election.”

The post also named a Maricopa County employee, who was previously targeted with similarly unfounded claims and threats back in 2021.

The video quickly racked up over 1 million views, boosted by figures like Kari Lake, the former TV star who is now a senior adviser in the Trump administration, who also boosted claims about election fraud in Maricopa County when she lost races in 2022 and 2024 for governor and the US Senate, respectively.

“More shenanigans at the Maricopa county ballot tabulation center,” Lake wrote on X. “Only through God’s intervention was this even discovered.”

But it wasn’t God who provided the video to the group. Jennifer Liewer, the deputy elections director for communications in Maricopa County tells WIRED that the clip was taken from a nonpublic backup livestream camera that is active but not currently one of the livestream cameras available on the county’s website. A source with knowledge of the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record tells WIRED that members of the We the People group had obtained the IP address for the camera years ago, allegedly allowing them to continue to monitor it. We the People did not respond to a request for comment.

The Maricopa County Board of Supervisors issued a statement last week that debunked the claim, clarifying that the employees were “performing authorized and necessary work to update software and upload election data to a computer terminal that is not connected to the internet or ballot tabulation equipment.”

Unsatisfied with this explanation, Shelby Busch, the founder of We The People USA Alliance and a representative for the Republican National Committee (RNC), then contacted the Maricopa County recorder Justin Heap, who is aligned with Trump. His office then contacted the FBI to investigate the issue, according to Heap’s chief of staff.

The FBI asked an investigator from the Arizona attorney general’s office to investigate, and they quickly concluded there was nothing to investigate, according to a copy of their report seen by 12News. “Election integrity is one of the top priorities of this FBI, and we continue to work around the clock to pursue criminal actors who seek to undermine our system and the rule of law,” the FBI tells WIRED.

The RNC and Busch did not respond to a request for comment.

The FBI’s closed investigation has not quelled the conspiracy theories. On Thursday, Busch appeared on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast repeating claims that something nefarious had happened, and that she had contacted the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice to investigate the matter further.

“Can somebody get involved here?” Bannon replied.

The Justice Department, DHS, and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.

“Election rumors contain the same, or very similar, narrative tropes that make them easily digestible for audiences and remixable for rumor producers,” says Starbird, whose group has created a bingo card of such tropes. “Maricopa County has become a trope, a suspicious setting, for election rumors. It’s a ready-to-use building block for a new rumor or conspiracy theory.”

entries.title: How Elizabeth Holmes Tricked WIRED—and Everyone Else
entries.summary: WIRED was the first magazine to cover Theranos and its enticing billionaire founder. There were warning signs even then.
entries.content:
Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of the fraud-ridden blood-test company Theranos, made her national press debut in The Wall Street Journal in 2013. The article—“A Drop of Blood, an Instant Diagnosis”—wasn’t a science story, or even a business story. It ran in the Opinion section, by a writer on the Journal’s editorial board named Joseph Rago, winner of a Pulitzer Prize for critiques of the Affordable Care Act.

He wrote that he was impressed by the prospect of individuals having more direct control of their health care; no less an eminence than former secretary of state George Shultz, a Theranos board member, had told Rago that Holmes was the next Steve Jobs or Bill Gates.

By 2014, Holmes was the youngest woman billionaire ever, and the mid-2010s were electric with tech-industry success stories—the iPhone, Tesla, Airbnb, Twitter. I was an editor at WIRED back then, and Theranos-as-presented felt very WIRED. It looked like evidence that a Silicon Valley approach to innovation would work in every industry, including medicine. And at the magazine that first published the idea of the “quantified self,” Theranos’ pitch validated the notion that individuals could take charge of their own health with innovative tech and access to data.

One of my colleagues, an editor named Caitlin Roper, saw a story in Theranos and in Holmes, but no one was sure what shape it should take. The executive editor suggested Roper just go talk to Holmes and see what was what. The result was an influential long-form Q&A headlined “One Drop, Infinite Data: How Elizabeth Holmes Built a Better Blood Test.” Because print magazines move with the agility and speed of a post-Panamax cargo ship, the story didn’t run until the March 2014 issue.

Over the next few months, other publications followed. Fortune put Holmes on the cover. The New Yorker did a profile. In October 2015, Inc. put her on the cover, calling her “the next Steve Jobs”—and a couple of weeks later, The Wall Street Journal did another article on Theranos, by the reporter John Carreyrou. The headline was deceptively humble: “Theranos Has Struggled with Blood Tests.”

Uh-oh.

The speedy and accurate blood tests were fake, the innovative tech didn’t exist, and Walgreens, a major partner, terminated its deal with Theranos. It was a grift. A new documentary film, out this week, follows Holmes in the weeks leading up to her incarceration.

Get a bunch of old WIRED editors together these days and it doesn’t take more than one drink before we start asking each other whether we enabled the worst parts of the tech world’s rise to power. Sometimes it seems like every antichrist-lecturing, panopticon-building, machine-god-bothering weirdo with $100 billion and a government contract made his debut in our pages. So, with Theranos and Holmes back in the news, the current administration at WIRED wondered what we were thinking back then.

It was a long time ago. I called Caitlin.

As always, we were looking for good stories. “I was interested in this female founder, but also the idea that her actual goal was disruption of health care, that there could be more transparency and reduced costs,” says Roper, who today is executive producer for scripted film and TV at The New York Times. “I was going through some medical stuff at the time and having constant blood tests, and I was curious about what this could do.”

Roper got a go-ahead to report and write something, execution to be determined. In the house jargon: Green light, format TK. She and I talked it through separately. “The conversation I remember with you, which I thought of many years later, was looking at the board of directors, her board, which was just completely batshit. It had military figures and government officials, and just seemed very odd,” Roper says. “You said there was something weird about that. It raised your suspicious hackles.”

It did—a few of us thought we saw hints of red flags. The company hadn’t published any peer-reviewed data. Colleagues had heard unconfirmable rumors of shenanigans inside the company. But that didn’t mean it wasn’t a story. We’d just have to figure out how to handle all that. WIRED had been, in years past, overly credulous, especially of scientific claims. But primarily WIRED covered innovation and stuff that sounded futuristic. This felt like it qualified.

“I remember that with dramatic irony, looking back,” Roper says.

Holmes agreed to an interview, and Roper went down to the Valley, to Theranos’ offices. She was only the second reporter to be there, and she got the performance that Holmes would become famous for. “There’s a lot of weird things about her. She was speaking in this strange, low voice. She was wearing a Steve Jobs outfit—black turtleneck,” Roper says. “She seemed like she was very precisely trying to project something.” (That first WSJ story ran with an illustrated caricature; WIRED shot a photo, professionally styled, of Holmes in her signature look.)

They spent an hour talking. Roper got her blood drawn, a tiny pinprick from the tip of her finger. “I said, ‘I’d love to see the box, can I follow my blood sample?’” Roper says. “They said, absolutely not.” Company reps implied it was a health-and-safety issue.

Instead, Holmes took Roper to the Palo Alto Walgreens, one of the few where Theranos had actually set up shop. “That part seemed like a snow job,” Roper says. “It was clear even from my own basic research that it hadn’t rolled out.” The booth at Walgreens was not in service. Holmes told her the company was going to open Walgreens labs across the Southwest.

Roper’s blood results came back. “The panel they took was similar to a panel I’d just had. I looked at them, and they matched,” Roper says. That seemed roughly confirmatory, at the time. It’s impossible to know now how it pulled that off, but later it turned out Theranos maintained a fully kitted-out lab in its Palo Alto offices, in addition to the lab for the company’s supposed new tech.

Interview done, Roper drove back up to San Francisco, to WIRED. “It didn’t feel like there was a feature to do,” she says. The Walgreens stuff wasn’t happening yet; it was too hard to report out how the technology worked. What was hard, in retrospect, was validation. Roper and the bosses weren’t sure that investment money from bold-faced names made up for an absence of hard scientific evidence.

So Roper wrote it up as an interview—a Q&A. “It seemed more like an interesting founder story,” she says. Roper asked every hard question, and got answers. They just turned out to be lies. But Roper acknowledges some cracks in the story’s origin. “If she had not been a woman, I would have been less motivated. That was part of what compelled me,” she says. “I felt sympathetic to the idea of her outfit and her weirdness, because I related to the idea that she was passing in some way in that environment, needing to assert herself.”

It’s tempting to see in that a DEI-run-amok story. It isn’t. All of us at WIRED were trying to wrestle with sexism in the world we covered, and at our magazine. Holmes’ board was all non–Silicon Valley types—was that because venture investors and scientists had identified her as a bad risk, or was it because Silicon Valley venture capitalists don’t support women founders?

Just a month after Roper’s Q&A ran, a team of researchers at the Harvard Business School and MIT Sloan School published a paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences showing that investors were far more likely to fund the same pitch if it came from a man than if it came from a woman—and that conventionally attractive men did even better. Today, roughly 75 percent of venture investors are men, and the proportions were worse a decade ago. There’s even research showing that male venture investors are more likely to promote women to partner if the men have daughters. Roper and WIRED were trying to fight that tide and ran aground on a grifter instead.

“Partially, yes, it’s a woman founder, and that’s a nice change of pace. It would’ve been nice if you guys could have beaten John Carreyrou and figured it out,” says Dave Karpf, an associate professor at George Washington University who has read every issue of WIRED and uses them to teach a class about Silicon Valley’s visions of the future. “But it wasn’t a new, untested claim. It was an active fraud.”

It’s fair to imagine a timeline where WIRED dug in deeper and was more critical, or at least didn’t further drive the hype cycle. “That story and the way we photographed her was absolutely fuel to lauding her and drawing attention,” Roper says. “I do feel partially responsible for that.”

We probably were, but I’m not sure WIRED’s Q&A was any more or less credulous than stories other magazines did. I know I sound defensive here, but even WIRED’s rigorous fact-check process wasn’t designed to unmask fraud. We all got got; it’s easy to see red flags when they’re in the rearview mirror. Was it weird to believe a 19-year-old college dropout had noticed something about pathology and microfluidics no one else had? Sure, but as Karpf points out, the system valorizes those kinds of iconoclasts. Steve Jobs was a dropout, man!

“If she had done all the graduate work, she wouldn’t have been nearly as fundable. They would just find someone else to tell them the stories they want to fund,” Karpf says. “It’s the people promoting it who, I think, have a bunch of answering to do.”

In 2019, as Sam Altman was leaving his role leading the tech incubator Y Combinator to become CEO of OpenAI, he wrote a blog post extolling the virtue in founders with “too much self belief … almost to the point of delusion.” Venture investors will tell you they invest in people as much as ideas, and the ideas are sometimes early-days, or half-baked. The system encourages exaggeration—right up to the line of deception. It can favor charismatic hucksters. If Theranos’ technology didn’t quite work yet, well, that’s a core tenet of Silicon Valley: Fake it till you make it.

And for a long time, WIRED helped. The magazine touted big ideas, and sometimes those ideas turned out to be dumb. Sometimes we were too early; sometimes we were wrong. Pitch meetings for stories big and small were a bit of a Thunderdome, actually. Eventually we developed some heuristics to encode skepticism in the process. For architecture stories, renders weren’t enough—ground had to have been broken. Physical objects had to exist in physical space; reporters had to be able to visit a thing. A flying car had to, you know, fly. In stories about new drugs or medical devices, the gating rule became “phase 3 trials or get the fuck out.”

Today, every responsible tech journalist has had to don new kinds of armor to prepare for the future that WIRED helped create. It’s possible to marvel at robot cars navigating cities as if driven by ghosts—while acknowledging the ways they sometimes fail, are often remote-piloted by humans, and pose new questions about regulating Big Tech. It’s possible to be awed by generative artificial intelligence’s capabilities while also interrogating the motives and practices of the companies that build it. And, yes, the personal politics of tech trillionaires matter when they’re donating more than a quarter of a billion dollars to support one political party over another. All of that was probably WIRED’s responsibility back then; it’s everyone’s responsibility now.

The tech business hates all that, reasonably. Not rarely, some longtime Silicon Valley dude will learn I spent most of my career at WIRED and say something like, “What happened to that place? I miss the old, optimistic WIRED.”

But you know, in the same issue of the magazine that carried the Holmes Q&A, another of our colleagues, Bill Wasik, wrote an opinion piece touted on the cover as “Silicon Valley’s Douchebag Problem.” Wasik, today the science editor at The New York Times, wrote then that dead-eyed misbehavior in pursuit of profit would kill tech’s magical status. Peter Thiel–derived ideas about secession and business models that relied on surveillance capitalism risked a backlash that would burn it all down, Wasik warned. The Valley and its toys, he wrote, would end up “a punch line—a hallucination of a future that no one believes in anymore.”

Science and tech journalism have to be about more than investors and returns. The future is too important; the stakes are too high. Case in point: As part of Joseph Rago’s reporting on Elizabeth Holmes and Theranos, he got his finger pricked. Rago’s blood test results were back “by the time I walked out the door,” he wrote. “(Phew: all clear.)” Four years later, Rago, 34, died alone in his New York apartment.

The city medical examiner said the cause of his death was sarcoidosis, a rare (and rarely fatal), hard-to-diagnose inflammatory disorder. Doctors usually figure it out by excluding other possibilities. Rago didn’t even know he had the disease. But among its signs are elevated levels of vitamin D and angiotensin-converting enzyme. Maybe an honest blood test would have spotted it.

entries.title: The Story of Billy Evans and ‘Theranos 2.0’
entries.summary: Elizabeth Holmes’ husband is a major figure in Nathan Fielder’s new documentary. But who is Billy Evans—and is he really working on a second blood-testing company?
entries.content:
Warning: Light movie spoilers below. Read at your own risk.

Even before becoming the stars of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s much-buzzed-about new documentary, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans were a special kind of couple. Holmes “may have ultimately failed to change the world in the way she set out,” Evans wrote in a letter at the time of Holmes’ sentencing in 2022, “but she has undeniably changed mine.” The Theranos founder, in the hardest years of her life, taught her husband “a patience” that he “would have previously dismissed as unnecessary and soft.”

She brought out his inner light, another sentencing letter from a friend of the couple reports: When they returned from a “monthslong camping trip,” Evans “displayed a new level of compassion in his demeanor, a strong sense of intention with his actions, and a heightened desire to listen to and look at others with purpose.” Whatever others might think, Evans was saying, Holmes wasn’t the only one of the pair that had been given a second chance. And they might get a second second chance with Haemanthus, a company that Evans is keen to reassure social media followers is absolutely—most definitely— “not Theranos 2.0.” A person familiar with the business told The Wall Street Journal that Holmes is not involved.

But viewers of You Can See Everything will watch Evans agreeing to the characterization that he and Holmes are making Theranos 2.0. They discuss the trajectory to make a working prototype of something on camera; they talk about collaborating on product ideas from prison. “To meet her, to spend time with her, that was the intention of the film,” the Austin, Texas-based Evans told David Friedberg, a cohost of the podcast All-In. “I haven’t seen it yet. I might think this is the dumbest thing that I have done.”

So who is Evans? And what is he building?

Long before fathering two children—son William and daughter Invicta—with Holmes, Evans grew up in San Diego in one of the city’s more prominent families, heir to midcentury pioneers in the Southern California tourism industry. His grandparents, William and Anne Evans were “two young hoteliers [who] saw the future,” according to the family’s company website, and opened up what would become a popular resort hotel on a mudflat in Mission Bay in 1953. They added a second nearby, and today own a third in La Jolla. This brought generational wealth. The business passed in part to Billy’s father, also named William.

Billy went to the Francis Parker School, one of the most prestigious private schools in the city. “The Evans family is very well respected in San Diego,” said a contemporary of Evans’ who worked for the family as a teenager, but Billy ““always a source of drama, would try to fight to start fights.” He had “affluenza” and was “just your classic spoiled rich kid” in a way that was not true of all his relatives. The inner light would come around later. (Evans did not want to be interviewed for the story and did not answer specific questions.)

After graduating from MIT with a bachelor of science in economics, Evans reportedly tried to launch a startup offering medical concierge services. This failed. He then took jobs in a handful of tech companies, including LinkedIn and Luminar Technologies, a self-driving car company. In 2017, at a “Fleet Week charity event” in the Bay Area, the then 25-year-old met Holmes and was “captivated,” he later wrote the judge at her sentencing, “by her childish wonder and authenticity.”

There was some reporting in the early years that the Evans family was not entirely enthused by this courtship, but doubts seemed to have dissipated by the time of the Holmes trial. Billy’s father, William Evans, showed up to the courtroom incognito, under the alias “Hanson,” identifying himself as a kind of mechanic. (He owns an enormous classic car collection.) To journalists, he defended Holmes’ honor. In court, he turned heads by unwrapping a “large Rice Krispies Treat” whose crinkling foil drowned out the judge on the first day of jury selection, NPR reported.

While in the film Evans and Holmes are both shown on fundraising calls, her name doesn’t appear in any of the incorporation documents of Haemanthus, the company Evans founded in 2022. There is little publicly available information on the company; to date, it has released no products and barely has a LinkedIn page, let alone a website. Yet its name can’t help but conjure up Theranos, and, indeed, its stated goal is to bring blood, urine, and saliva testing to American homes in the form of a countertop-size machine, which was more or less the goal of Theranos.

But the technology of Haemanthus seems to be a bit different than that of Theranos. Where the earlier company’s machine hoped to perfect the “miniaturization” of existing diagnostic techniques such that they could fit in a box on a counter, using a very small blood sample, Haemanthus’ machine uses “light.” To employ a cooler word, it uses lasers. The company’s Raman Spectroscopy System, a patent for which was granted January 21, 2025, suggests a machine capable of firing high-power light sources into biological samples and reading the resulting information accurately.

Raman Spectroscopy is a real and promising diagnostic tool and the subject of research since its discovery by, among others, C. V. Raman in 1928. Shine a light source at a material and perhaps one in 1 million photons will shift in frequency in relation to the molecular vibrations of the material it bounced off of. That shift can be measured and analyzed, and a century of work has gone into making this process a little easier and a little more useful, carried out today by specialists at research universities and hospitals.

It may someday be even more useful. WIRED contacted Eric Potma, a professor of chemistry at UC Irvine, to shed some light on the technology. “Given that I act as one of their consultants, I am not sure if it is appropriate for me to delve much further into this,” he wrote back. “All I can say is that from an engineering perspective, they have some interesting ideas that are worth exploring.”

“It is not a technology concept pulled out of thin air, as people may be inclined to think based on the fact that the company is run by Elizabeth's husband (and thus an automatic repeat of the Theranos story),” he continued over email. “My own assessment is that Haemanthus is not Theranos. The engineers at Haemanthus are legit, and they are really trying to push the Raman detection technology into interesting directions.”

The challenges of putting this highly sensitive and difficult diagnostic technique into home appliances able to assess human health markers with a level of accuracy in seconds that will pass regulatory scrutiny—as promised in the company’s promotional materials—are great, though. Last year, The New York Times said that the company had garnered a $3.5 million investment from “friends and family.” It now reports as much as $20 million in funding.

Press accounts of the company’s marketing materials seem to promise investors that the company faces “no regulatory oversight,” in part because the machine would only be developed to test veterinary diseases at first. The New York Times, though, confirmed with the USDA that the agency had regulatory oversight over “vet diagnostics.”

Evans told the Times, which had other questions, that the company was “in stealth” and would remain so: “They aren’t going to find anything associated with the name Haemanthus.” There are a few things out there, among them the patent, but stealth mode continues. The addresses that turn up are mostly connected to private homes in one of Austin’s more desirable neighborhoods, near Barton Springs. Contacted by phone, a few folks who seem likely to be employees of the company declined to talk or even confirm or deny their role.

The desire for “stealth,” though, is a little discordant with the desire to participate in a yearslong documentary project with a graduate of one of Canada’s top business schools. Perhaps it will help raise money: Once the laser system is perfected, the company hopes, according to materials reviewed by the Times, to put the whole thing in a stamp-size wearable device, a research process it told investors will take “three years and $70 million.” Holmes will be reportedly moving from prison to a halfway house next summer. The world may yet be changed.
